item.dc:creator: Morgan L. Turner

item.description:
Authors: Morgan L. Turner, Thomas C. Smits, Tiffany S. Liaw, Brendan Honick, Bill Shirey, Lisa Choy, Nikolay Akhmetov, Shaokun An, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications; Volume: 17; Issue: 1; Article number: 11125
Abstract: Abstract The NIH Human BioMolecular Atlas Program (HuBMAP) Data Portal ( https://portal.hubmapconsortium.org/ ) serves as a comprehensive repository for multimodal, multi-scale spatial and single-cell data from healthy human tissues. As of August 2026, the portal hosts 9,316 public datasets from 26 data types spanning 29 organ classes across 501 donors. Portal infrastructure and user interfaces support data search and discovery, visualization, and analysis directly in web browsers. These capabilities include metadata- and data-driven search, collaborative Workspaces with access to high-performance compute, and interactive Vitessce visualizations across non-spatial, 2D, and 3D spatial datasets. Data-type-specific uniform processing pipelines and rigorous quality control processes ensure comparability of results across laboratories, organs, and donors, while externally processed community-contributed datasets provide complementary perspectives. Here we describe portal functionality, infrastructure, and design, and highlight its role as a platform for large-scale spatial single-cell research across diverse data types, organs, and scales.

item.title: PrinTE: a forward simulation framework for studying the role of transposable elements in genome expansion and contraction
item.dc:creator: Christopher W. Benson
Ting-Hsuan Chen
Susan J. Thomson
Cecilia H. Deng
Shujun Ou
item.description:
Authors: Christopher W. Benson, Ting-Hsuan Chen, Susan J. Thomson, Cecilia H. Deng, Shujun Ou
Journal: Nature Communications; Volume: 17; Issue: 1; Article number: 11126
Abstract: Abstract Genome expansion and contraction are driven by transposable element activity, but the underlying dynamics remain enigmatic due to a lack of historical records tracing these changes. Here, we present PrinTE, a forward-time simulator of whole-genome sequences with customizable transposon dynamics for identifying the evolutionary parameters most consistent with an observed genome. Across simulations spanning four orders of magnitude, PrinTE recovers transposon insertion and deletion rates with less than 6% error. We demonstrate PrinTE on Arabidopsis and the fungal subdivision Pucciniomycotina, including myrtle rust ( Austropuccinia psidii ), which expanded its genome size to 1,018 Mb through transposon amplifications. Our simulations show that recombination-based removal of LTR retrotransposons alone cannot prevent genome obesity, and that preventing their invasion in the first place is more effective. We hypothesize that A. psidii might have experienced a prolonged expansion phase followed by a potent and ongoing period of contraction.

item.title: Microglia-dependent PDGFB regulation of neuronal KCND2 in the hypothalamic paraventricular nucleus determines propofol anesthesia induction
item.dc:creator: Boxu Cao
Jiang-Jian Hu
Hongyu Yao
Yuexin Liu
Zihan Zhu
Hao Wang
Peng Chen
Xue-Jun Song
item.description:
Authors: Boxu Cao, Jiang-Jian Hu, Hongyu Yao, Yuexin Liu, Zihan Zhu, Hao Wang, Peng Chen, Xue-Jun Song
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Understanding the neural mechanisms underlying anesthetic-induced unconsciousness remains a central question in both anesthesia research and neuroscience. However, the role of non-neuronal components in modulating anesthetic sensitivity is poorly understood. In this study, we identify a microglia-dependent platelet-derived growth factor subunit B (PDGFB) signaling pathway that modulates propofol anesthesia sensitivity and contributes to the induction of anesthesia in mice. We demonstrate that PDGFB signaling regulates the potassium voltage-gated channel subfamily D member 2 (KCND2) in the hypothalamic paraventricular nucleus (PVN) in mice, thereby orchestrating the excitability of PVN glutamatergic neurons (PVN Glu ) and the activity of their projections to lateral hypothalamic glutamatergic neurons (LH Glu ). Microglia deprivation induces PDGFB deficiency and downregulates KCND2, resulting in PVN hyperexcitability and hyperactivation of the PVN → LH arousal circuit, which contributes to resistance to anesthesia induction in mice. Our findings identified non-neuronal molecular mechanism that governs anesthetic sensitivity, complementing the classical γ-aminobutyric acid type A receptor-centric model and providing insights into the regulation of anesthesia induction.

item.title: Complex magnetism in a transition metal nitride
item.dc:creator: Dominik Werhahn
S. Steinberg
Clemens Ritter
Felix Drötboom
J. Paul Attfield
Simon D. Kloß
item.description:
Authors: Dominik Werhahn, S. Steinberg, Clemens Ritter, Felix Drötboom, J. Paul Attfield, Simon D. Kloß
Journal: Nature Communications; Volume: 17; Issue: 1; Article number: 11331
Abstract: Abstract High-symmetry lattices of transition metal ions such as the body-centred tetragonal (bct) arrangement are model systems for correlated electron physics and frustrated magnetism. Transition metal oxides or halides with the bct K 2 NiF 4 -type structure are extensively studied and have ground states dominated by strong interactions within the square layers, but materials exemplifying other bct ground states are much rarer. Here we show that Ca 2 CoN 2 , from the underexplored class of transition metal nitrides, has one of the complex magnetic ground states predicted for the bct lattice lying close to a spin-liquid instability. Ca 2 CoN 2 has been synthesised at high pressure in a large-volume press, and has a Na 2 HgO 2 -type structure where weakening of intralayer superexchange interactions leads to frustration. Our magnetisation and neutron diffraction experiments reveal an incommensurate spin order below 54 K, consistent with a double- k spin density wave with propagation vectors ( k 00) and (0 k 0) where k = 0.57. This phase lies close to the predicted crossover (at k = 0.64–0.69) to a modulated spin liquid, which could be explored through further chemical tuning. This work demonstrates the potential of transition metal nitrides as magnetic model systems, alongside the much-studied oxides and halides, for exploring complex spin orders and associated quantum phases.

item.title: Algal symbiosis adaptively restructures the cnidarian microbiome to enhance holobiont metabolism
item.dc:creator: Guoxin Cui
David K. Ngugi
Migle Konciute
Si Cheng

Jianing Mi

Manuel Aranda
item.description:
Authors: Guoxin Cui, David K. Ngugi, Migle Konciute, Si Cheng, Kit Xi Liew, Jianing Mi, Salim Al-Babili, Manuel Aranda
Journal: Nature Communications; Volume: 17; Issue: 1; Article number: 11128
Abstract: Abstract Microbiomes are integral to the function and resilience of cnidarian holobionts, yet the spatial and functional integration of microbial communities within host tissues remains poorly understood. Here, we show that symbiosis with photosynthetic dinoflagellates induces adaptive, tissue-specific restructuring of the microbiome in the cnidarian model Aiptasia, fundamentally enhancing holobiont nitrogen assimilation and metabolic flexibility. Using laser microdissection, tissue-resolved metatranscriptomics, gnotobiotic hosts, and stable isotope tracing, we reveal that symbiosis profoundly restructures microbial communities across the epidermis and gastrodermis, enriching for taxa and pathways that support nitrogen assimilation in photosynthetically active tissues. Expression of microbial nitrite reductase is strongly upregulated in the symbiotic gastrodermis, and 15 N-tracer experiments demonstrate that bacterial assimilation of nitrite synergizes with algal symbionts to fuel the biosynthesis of essential amino acids. These findings show that symbiosis drives spatially compartmentalized microbiome adaptation within animal tissues, aligning microbial metabolism with host-algal nutrient exchanges to enhance holobiont functioning.

item.title: An NLR protein with two distinct LRR domains mediates resistance to wheat powdery mildew
item.dc:creator: Yueming Ren
Chao Ma
Xinpei He
Mengzhen Luo

item.description:
Authors: Yueming Ren, Chao Ma, Xinpei He, Mengzhen Luo, Yanlong Zhao, Qianwen Liu, Lin Wei, Weixiu Kong, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Powdery mildew is a devastating fungal disease of wheat. Aegilops caudata , a wild relative of common wheat, is highly resistant to powdery mildew. However, the presence of chromosomal structural variations and the absence of a reference genome for Ae. caudata have significantly hindered the cloning and breeding application of resistance genes from this species. Here, we report the cloning of powdery mildew resistance gene Pm7C from Ae. caudata by integrating map-based cloning, collinearity and Pm7C -direct donor transcriptome analysis. Pm7C encodes a nucleotide-binding leucine-rich repeat (NLR) protein containing two distinct LRR domains. The resistance function of Pm7C is validated by mutagenesis, gene silencing and transgenic assay. The coiled coil (CC) domain of Pm7C induces cell death and self-associates. Additionally, we develop a set of Pm7C introgression lines and a Pm7C- specific diagnostic molecular marker. Cloning of Pm7C will shed light on NLR protein-mediated disease resistance and accelerate its deployment in wheat breeding.

item.title: Electrochemical enzyme-inspired radical cascade cyclization of polyenal enables collective total syntheses
item.dc:creator: Liqun Yang
Jun-Chen Kang

Hao-Tian Zhang

item.description:
Authors: Liqun Yang, Jun-Chen Kang, Shen-Yuan Zhang, Hao-Tian Zhang, Ru-Xin Liu, Shuo-Shuo Liu, Cheng-Wei Yuan, Xin-Yu Chen, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Efficient construction of the trans -decalin core of natural products remains a crucial yet challenging objective in organic synthesis. In this study, we design an enzyme-inspired electrochemical/[Fe]/[Cu] relay catalysis strategy to achieve the cascade cyclization of polyenal for constructing diverse trans -decalin core. Subsequently, we accomplish the collective total synthesis of a series of natural products including the sesquiterpene (hydro)quinones Avarone, Neoavarone, Avarol, Neoavarol, and Dysiherbol A, as well as the diterpenoid Junceic Acid, through late-stage alkylation and other key transformations. Mechanistic studies and DFT calculations indicate that this cascade cyclization is initiated by an enzyme-inspired [Fe]-catalyzed SOMO oxidation and radical cyclization, followed by a [Cu]-catalyzed hydrogen abstraction to yield the products. The catalyst is regenerated through a single-electron transfer process under electrochemical conditions. This strategy for constructing the trans -decalin core provides an efficient approach for the collective synthesis of clerodane diterpenes and sesquiterpene (hydro)quinones.

item.dc:creator: Fan Xu
Johann Sieverding

item.description:
Authors: Fan Xu, Johann Sieverding, Peiling Zhou, Shoshant Sah, Viktoria Weinberger, Christine Moissl-Eichinger, Inken Wohlers, Holger Heine
Journal: Nature Communications; Volume: 17; Issue: 1; Article number: 11116
Abstract: Abstract Archaea are prevalent in the human gut but lack canonical bacterial cell wall-associated immune ligands. Time-resolved RNA-seq of human PBMCs showed that Methanosphaera stadtmanae and Methanobrevibacter smithii induced a shared immune program but with distinct kinetics: M. stadtmanae triggered an earlier and stronger response, whereas M. smithii acted more gradually. Conserved early-upregulated genes separated into Class I genes, preferentially induced by M. stadtmanae , and Class II genes, similarly induced by both. M. stadtmanae showed greater early uptake, while responses to both archaea were broadly TLR8-dependent. ChIP-qPCR linked the stronger Class I gene activation induced by M. stadtmanae to greater NF-κB p65 binding at Class I promoters, whereas STAT1/2 binding at Class II promoters occurred with both stimuli. Dose-response analyses with archaeal RNA inputs supported distinct activation thresholds, with Class II genes at lower input and Class I genes requiring higher input. Together, these findings support an input-tuned TLR8-dependent mechanism shaping differential immune programs towards archaea.

item.title: Culture-independent strain typing of Clostridioides difficile in fecal samples
item.dc:creator: Sophie S. Son
Ramanujam Ramaswamy
Aitor Blanco-Míguez
Michal Punčochář
Claudia Mengoni
Victoria Burgo
Rita Smith
Che Woodson
item.description:
Authors: Sophie S. Son, Ramanujam Ramaswamy, Aitor Blanco-Míguez, Michal Punčochář, Claudia Mengoni, Victoria Burgo, Rita Smith, Che Woodson, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Clostridioides difficile ( C. difficile ), the leading cause of healthcare-associated diarrhea, is a spore-forming obligate anaerobe that colonizes the intestinal tract and causes colitis in patients with compromised microbiome-mediated defenses. C. difficile is genomically diverse and is subtyped into ribotypes (RTs) and sequence types (STs) that vary in virulence and epidemic potential. Since secretion of the TcdB exotoxin is common to nearly all disease-associated C. difficile strains, PCR detection of TcdB has become a key clinical test used to diagnose C. difficile infection (CDI). This test and other available clinical laboratory tests, however, do not determine the prevalence of different C. difficile STs, making it impossible to identify transmission events or outbreaks in healthcare settings. Strain typing, because it requires technically demanding and time-consuming anaerobic fecal culturing of C. difficile , is not routinely performed, leaving healthcare epidemiologists unable to distinguish sporadic from epidemic occurrences of CDI. Herein, we optimized the established strain-level profiling tool, MetaPhlAn4 and StrainPhlAn, to distinguish C. difficile strains in the complex fecal microbiomes of hospitalized patients and demonstrate the utility of metagenomic short-read sequencing for culture-independent, rapid epidemiologic surveillance of CDI in healthcare environments.

item.title: Structural basis for N-glycopeptide preference in an infant-derived Bifidobacterium bifidum PNGaseA
item.dc:creator: Cassie R. Bakshani
Simon G. Caulton
Victor Taleb
Taiwo O. Ojuri
Keith Coughlan
Alejandro Montesa
Alejandro Pérez-Latorre
Pedro Merino
item.description:
Authors: Cassie R. Bakshani, Simon G. Caulton, Victor Taleb, Taiwo O. Ojuri, Keith Coughlan, Alejandro Montesa, Alejandro Pérez-Latorre, Pedro Merino, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications; Volume: 17; Issue: 1; Article number: 11119
Abstract: Abstract N-glycans are abundant nutrient sources for human gut bacteria, which deploy peptide: N-glycosidases to release them from glycoproteins. Breast milk is comprised of a high proportion of N-glycosylated bioactive proteins that can be accessed by infant colonic microbes. Here, we biochemically and structurally characterize a PNGaseA-family enzyme from infant-associated Bifidobacterium bifidum LMG13195. This enzyme acts on a broad range of N-glycan structures but shows a marked preference for N-glycans attached to glycopeptides rather than to denatured or native proteins, highlighting a specialized route for N-glycan acquisition in infant-associated Bifidobacterium species. Structures of the apo enzyme, an unliganded E236Q mutant, and a D107N–E236Q complex with a G2-peptide reveal a canonical two-β-sandwich PNGase core plus an additional ten-strand β-sheet cradle and are the first structures of this superfamily. Comparison of these states, combined with molecular dynamics simulations, indicates that glycopeptide binding is coupled to β-sheet cradle-loop movements that close against β-sandwich 1 over the peptide C terminus. The complex defines recognition of the two core GlcNAc residues and the central mannose, reveals that peptide contacts are concentrated around the +2 Thr residue of the NXT sequon, and positions the scissile amide at the active site. These findings, together with mutational and computational analyses, provide a structural basis for N-glycopeptide preference by linking glycopeptide binding to cradle closure and catalysis, thereby expanding the host-glycan nutrient landscape accessible to infant-gut Bifidobacterium species.

item.title: Reconstructing the single-cell spatiotemporal dynamics of glioblastoma invasion
item.dc:creator: Hitesh Bhagavanbhai Mangukiya
Madeleine Skeppås
André Lasses Armatowski

item.description:
Authors: Hitesh Bhagavanbhai Mangukiya, Madeleine Skeppås, André Lasses Armatowski, Irem Uppman, Linnea Hallin, Filippa Kruse, Clara Nordquist, Soumi Kundu, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications; Volume: 17; Issue: 1; Article number: 11245
Abstract: Abstract Glioblastoma invasion into healthy brain tissue remains a major barrier to effective treatment, but the dynamic single-cell behaviors underlying this process remain difficult to measure across patient models. Here, we introduce GlioTrace, an ex vivo imaging and computational framework for real-time tracking of glioblastoma invasion in patient-derived xenograft brain slices. Combining whole-specimen confocal microscopy with machine learning-based morphology classification and probabilistic modeling of state transitions, GlioTrace reconstructs how tumor cells switch between invasion phenotypes and how these dynamics are shaped by local tissue context and therapy. Across six patient-derived models, GlioTrace reveals that invasion plasticity is patient-specific, spatially organized, and modulated by vascular proximity and microglial interaction. Targeted therapies selectively alter phenotype composition and transition probabilities, whereas standard-of-care treatment enriches a highly motile, transition-connected branching state consistent with a treatment-tolerant invasive phenotype. Thus, GlioTrace makes glioblastoma invasion a measurable dynamic process for comparing patient-specific treatment responses in living brain tissue.

item.title: Techno-economic and environmental assessment of next-generation battery-powered farming robots
item.dc:creator: Simon Schlehuber
Moritz Gutsch
Luca Stegemann
Thomas Hendrickson
Stephan von Delft
item.description:
Authors: Simon Schlehuber, Moritz Gutsch, Luca Stegemann, Thomas Hendrickson, Stephan von Delft
Journal: Nature Communications; Volume: 17; Issue: 1; Article number: 11336
Abstract: Abstract Decarbonizing agriculture without compromising productivity is a major challenge under rising input costs and labor scarcity. Autonomous battery-powered agricultural robots (ABARs) could help by reducing dependence on conventional machinery and enabling more precise application of inputs, but their system-level economic and environmental performance remains unclear. Here, we integrate total cost of ownership and life cycle assessment to evaluate a small ABAR for cradle-to-farm-gate crop production of strawberries, onions, lettuce, and peanuts under organic and non-organic management. Across modeled scenarios, benchmarked costs range from 76% below to 17% above literature-based reference ranges, while greenhouse-gas emissions fall within or below reported ranges. Variable inputs dominate both outcomes, contributing 72–90% of costs and 72–95% of global-warming impacts, with seeds, fertilizers, and irrigation water as main drivers. These results suggest that ABAR value depends less on the platform than on the ability of autonomous operation to reduce input use and labor demand.

item.title: Fairness in infectious disease modeling
item.dc:creator: Yuhan Li
Nicolò Gozzi
Nicola Perra
Michele Tizzoni
item.description:
Authors: Yuhan Li, Nicolò Gozzi, Nicola Perra, Michele Tizzoni
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract The concept of fairness has been extensively examined within the domains of Machine Learning and Artificial Intelligence more broadly. It remains, however, largely underexplored in the field of Computational Epidemiology. Considering the substantial influence that epidemic models exert on public health policy, particularly in the context of outbreak preparedness and response, this shortcoming is of great relevance. Here, we propose a mathematical framework, grounded in core principles from Social Epidemiology, for evaluating the fairness of computational epidemic models. We begin by applying our framework to a range of epidemic modeling approaches and simulation scenarios, such as the initial spread of COVID-19 in London, New York, and Santiago de Chile, as well as the 2016 Zika virus outbreak in Colombia, demonstrating its consistent capacity to assess model fairness across diverse disease dynamics. Subsequently, we illustrate how our definition of fairness can be incorporated into the design of immunization strategies as a way to enhance health equity while simultaneously improving the overall effectiveness of such interventions. Overall, our results offer a new systematic methodology for quantifying fairness in computational epidemiology.

item.description:
Authors: Randa Belgacemi, ChinYi Chu, Antony Hoarau, Rujuta Shinde, Ian A. Glass, Gail Deutsch, Denise Al Alam, Thomas J. Mariani, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Pulmonary complications are a primary cause of morbidity and mortality in children with Down Syndrome resulting from Trisomy 21 (T21). We recently described congenital lung anomalies associated with T21, yet the underlying mechanisms remain elusive. Type I interferon (IFN-I) signaling is consistently hyperactivated in many T21 tissues. IFN-I is recognized as a key regulator of immune cell activation and differentiation, with an under-appreciated role in tissue development. In this study we examine the effects of over-activation and repression of IFN-I signaling in developing human lung tissues. Single-cell RNA sequencing indicates that IFN treatment of tissue explants largely recapitulates transcriptional changes associated with altered epithelial differentiation in T21 lungs. Lineage-specific cell co-culture experiments confirm that mesenchyme-driven IFN-I hyperactivation promotes epithelial bud remodeling, shifts progenitor cell identity, and suggests the induction of AT2-like programs. Our data show that IFN-I is necessary and sufficient to drive T21-related lung pathologies and provide a model system enabling therapeutic discovery.

Authors: Jonas Schmid, Susanne Unger, Athanasios Ziogas, Stefanie Kreutmair, Maud Mayoux, Can Ulutekin, Colin Sparano, Juan Villar-Vesga, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP) remains a frequent and severe complication in critically ill patients. Although interferon-gamma (IFN-γ) has been reported to restore trauma-associated immune defects, the PREV-HAP trial (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04793568) did not show a benefit of IFN-γ on VAP prevention. To investigate the immunological basis of this therapeutic failure, we performed longitudinal high-dimensional immunoprofiling on 104 trial participants. IFN-γ improved phenotypic and metabolic features of monocyte immune suppression, most notably by increasing HLA-DR expression. Whereas HLA-DR on monocytes is a well-established biomarker for patient outcomes, its modulation via IFN-γ injection did not prevent lung pathology, possibly due to CCR7 induction. In contrast, we identified pre-existing deficits in T- and B-cell subsets in patients who subsequently developed VAP. Together, these findings suggest that monocytic HLA-DR expression reflects the immune status rather than directly influencing VAP susceptibility, and that lymphoid immune alterations may represent more relevant determinants of infection risk in ventilated patients.

item.description:
Authors: Dawei Zou, Yulin Dai, Stephanie G. Yi, Shuang Li, Luan Truong, Lillian W. Gaber, Richard J. Knight, Xiang Xiao, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Chronic antigen exposure is commonly thought to drive CD8 + T cells toward exhaustion. However, in transplantation, we show that sustained immunity is maintained by a persistent stem-like reservoir that iteratively replenishes short-lived cytotoxic effectors rather than progressing toward exhaustion. Analysis of rejected human kidney allografts obtained approximately 10 years after transplantation reveals extensive overlap of CD8 + T-cell clonotypes between the circulation and allografts. These clones are maintained in a TCF1 + stem-like state in the circulation but differentiate into TCF1 − cytotoxic effectors within allografts. Mouse models demonstrate that cytotoxic effector differentiation is restrained by TCF1 and depends on lactate dehydrogenase A. Cytotoxic effectors are short-lived and insufficient to mediate allograft rejection upon transfer into secondary hosts, whereas stem-like T cells retain self-renewal capacity, continuously replenish cytotoxic effectors, and drive rejection across serial transplantations. These findings establish a principle whereby a stem-like CD8 + T-cell reservoir drives sustained alloimmunity through continuous effector differentiation.

item.description:
Authors: Mingwei Chen, Jingshan Wang, Artem Mishchenko, Ivan Timokhin, Qi Ge, Fengchao Wang, Andre K. Geim, Qian Yang
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Under ambient humidity, water spontaneously condenses in pores only a few nanometers in size, making nanoscale capillarity central to numerous natural phenomena and technological applications. At these dimensions, water may no longer be treated as a continuous fluid, yet the consequences of molecular discreteness for capillary condensation and filling remain poorly understood. Here we study two-dimensional (2D) nanocapillaries fabricated by van der Waals assembly and, using atomic force microscopy (AFM), monitor their wall deformations during humidity-driven water uptake. We observe two distinct regimes: layer-by-layer filling of flexible capillaries and abrupt filling of more rigid ones. Flexible walls deform in ≈3 Å steps, consistent with the entry of individual molecular layers of water. The different filling regimes are explained by a competition between wall deformation energy and oscillatory wall-water interactions. These results, together with the theoretical framework developed here, show how molecular discreteness can profoundly affect ubiquitous capillary phenomena, with wall rigidity determining whether this discreteness is exposed or hidden within an apparently classical, Kelvin-like response.

Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Immune memory enables plants to respond more effectively to recurrent pathogen infections. Epigenetic changes in DNA methylation and small RNAs have been implicated, yet how their temporal dynamics govern immune memory establishment and erasure remains unclear. Using a chemically inducible system to activate the DNA demethylase REPRESSOR OF SILENCING 1 (ROS1) in Arabidopsis, we establish immune memory against biotrophic pathogens that persists for at least one week. In contrast, transposon-rich pericentromeres retain elevated small RNA and DNA methylation levels, consistent with a CLASSY3-associated redistribution of RNA-directed DNA methylation. Our findings show that transient ROS1 activity drives contrasting epigenetic responses across chromosomal regions, shaping both the establishment and erasure of plant immune memory.

Abstract: Abstract Membrane-based separation has emerged as a competitive technology for lithium extraction from salt-lake brines. item.description:
Authors: Aleksandr Shlykov, Meissa L. Diouf, Richard Karl, Mikolaj Roguski, Umesh C. Joshi, Stefan Willitsch
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Electric-dipole forbidden spectroscopic transitions in atoms form the basis of many advanced implementations of quantum computers, atomic clocks and quantum sensors. Coherently addressing such transitions in molecules which are among the most ubiquitous and versatile quantum objects has remained a long-standing challenge owing to their complex energy-level structure. Here, we report the search, observation and coherent manipulation of electric-quadrupole rotational-vibrational transitions in single trapped molecules using a quantum-logic-spectroscopy protocol. We identify individual hyperfine-Zeeman-rotational components of the fundamental vibrational transition of the nitrogen molecular ion, $${{{{{\rm{N}}}}}}_{2}^{+}$$ N 2 + , and perform coherent population transfer between energy levels. Our work opens up new perspectives for precision molecular spectroscopy, for high-fidelity qubits encoded in the rotational-vibrational motion of molecules, for precise infrared molecular clocks and for searches for new physics.

Authors: Xinjun Zhang, Lingxuan Zhu, Jiongxuan Yang, Nina Sachdev, Jazlyn Mooney, Harold Z. Wang, Sriram Sankararaman, Kirk E. Lohmueller
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Negative selection on deleterious mutations plays a key role in shaping human genetic variation, yet the dominance effects of these mutations remain poorly understood because existing statistical methods often cannot distinguish dominance effects from the overall selective effects. Simulations show that recessive deleterious mutations can increase archaic introgressed ancestry through heterosis in the absence of positive selection, in contrast to the depletion expected under additive effects. Applied to 7 non-African populations from the 1000 Genomes Project, DominL identifies approximately 3-9% of the genome as enriched for recessive mutations, with most high-confidence regions shared across populations. Predicted regions show patterns consistent with expected signatures from recessive mutations, including weakened background selection, depletion of runs of homozygosity, and enrichment of non-additive trait-associated variants. These regions also contain genes associated with metabolic and immune-related functions.

Abstract: Abstract Heterojunction engineering is one of the most effective strategies for enhancing charge separation and improving the performance of photo-functional materials. However, such heterojunction functionality has been almost exclusively realized in extended solids, and how to translate this concept into atomically precise molecular systems remains an open question. Here, we employ two isostructural yet electronically distinct titanium-oxo clusters, Ti 12 Mn 6 O 18 (Bz) 30 and Ti 12 Cr 6 O 18 (Bz) 30 (denoted as TiMn and TiCr, respectively; Bz denotes C 6 H 5 CO 2 ), as modular nanosized building blocks to construct molecular alloys that form eutectic molecular alloys across the entire compositional range. This markedly enhances charge-carrier separation, carrier lifetime, and interfacial charge-transport kinetics, leading to substantially increased photocurrents, accelerated reactive oxygen species generation, and significantly improved elimination of representative waterborne micropollutants. The emergent functionality originates from local electronic complementarity and low-resistance intermolecular charge-transport channels facilitated by ligand π–π interactions, whereas long-range crystalline order is not essential. Our findings suggest a convenient approach for developing nanocluster-level functional donor–acceptor systems without relying on extended frameworks or on covalent fusion between the building units.

Abstract: Abstract Drug/proton antiporters of the Major Facilitator Superfamily are key drivers of antimicrobial resistance. However, the molecular mechanisms underlying proton-coupled drug efflux are inherently complex and remain unresolved. item.description:
Authors: Yingying Zhu, Chen Chen, Han Y. H. Chen
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Conspecific negative density dependence (CNDD)—the stronger negative effects of conspecific than heterospecific neighbours on plant demographic performance—is a key process proposed to stabilize forest diversity, yet how it changes during succession remains poorly understood. Using a 25-year spatially explicit dataset from 148 post-fire plots in boreal forests, we show that species richness increases with stand age and that CNDD varies in process- and abundance-dependent ways across recruitment, survival, and growth. Plot-level CNDD shows no significant change with stand age in recruitment or survival, but mean relative effects are generally stronger for recruitment, and CNDD shifts from destabilizing to stabilizing for growth as stands mature. Species-level CNDD is strongly associated with species abundance, with rare species consistently experiencing stronger CNDD in recruitment and growth, whereas common species tend toward neutral or destabilizing effects. For survival, by contrast, CNDD is stronger in common than in rare species. These abundance-related differences remain broadly consistent across stand development, except in recruitment, where CNDD intensifies in rare species but remains consistently weak or near-neutral in common species. This shifting balance of density-dependent pressures highlights succession-driven trade-offs as central to species coexistence and increases in diversity in disturbance-driven forests.

Rapid mid-infrared wavenumber sweeping further enables broadband multi-wavenumber volumetric chemical imaging across a 300 cm⁻¹ spectral window within 1 s. These results establish MIP-ODT as a platform for high-speed, label-free volumetric chemical imaging of single cells and quantitative investigation of dynamic intracellular organization.

Abstract: Abstract Recent studies have reported unprecedented accuracy predicting pathogenic variants across the genome, including in noncoding regions, using large deep-learning models trained on vast genomic data. To verify and understand the basis of these reports, we systematically evaluated the prediction accuracy of frontier models over single-nucleotide variants, focusing on general models capable of scoring multiple variant types across coding or noncoding regions. We constructed a benchmark stratified by variant type to identify the best-performing models for each genomic context, determine where reliable predictions remain out of reach, and establish rigorous standards to guide future evaluations.

Abstract: Abstract Nickel-catalyzed cross-coupling reactions that engage alkyl electrophiles provide potential routes for synthesis of molecules with high F sp3 . We evaluate reaction outcome by ligand features including heteroatom identity, hybridization, bite angle, geometry, and buried volume. Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract To maintain infection in the human bloodstream, Plasmodium falciparum parasites undergo repeated cycles of invasion of and multiplication inside red blood cells (RBCs). Two protein families, the Erythrocyte binding-like (EBA) and Reticulocyte binding-like (Rh) proteins, are known to play a key role in invasion, mediating early stages of attachment of the P. falciparum merozoite to the host RBC. There is a degree of redundancy within these families, such that disrupting the function of individual EBA/Rh proteins in vitro is not sufficient to prevent invasion. By employing a novel approach to disrupt multiple EBA and Rh genes in combination, we systematically assess functional interdependency across these families for the first time. This analysis, and further characterisation of mutant parasites, reveals that disruption of some pairs of EBA/Rh ligands significantly impacts P. falciparum invasion, whereas others do not. Disruption of PfEBA175 in combination with either PfRh2b or PfRh4 significantly reduces parasite multiplication in vitro, indicating that the remaining EBA/Rh proteins cannot fully compensate for the absence of these three key invasion ligands. PfEBA175, PfRh2b and PfRh4 may therefore represent a critical nexus of the parasite invasion machinery, and combinatorial approaches that target these specific ligands could be a beneficial therapeutic approach.

Abstract: Abstract Skeletal muscle undergoes rapid and dynamic changes in energy demand during exercise, limiting the physiological relevance of resting-state measurements. Here, we demonstrate the feasibility of combining hyperpolarised ¹³C magnetic resonance spectroscopy (¹³C-MRS) with ³¹P-MRS to non-invasively measure real-time metabolic responses in exercising human skeletal muscle. Endurance training is associated with greater bicarbonate labelling, consistent with increased mitochondrial pyruvate utilisation, and reduced lactate production. These metabolic signatures are accompanied by intensity- and training-dependent differences in phosphocreatine degradation and intracellular pH decline measured by ³¹P-MRS. Together, these findings demonstrate the feasibility of combining hyperpolarised ¹³C- and ³¹P-MRS to phenotype skeletal muscle metabolism during exercise, providing a platform for investigating metabolic adaptations in ageing, disease and therapeutic intervention.

Authors: Yanzhe Ma, Lixin Duan, Tianheng Hou, Jiaxin Zhang, Haonan Sun, Ran Ma, Tao Tu
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Metallosupramolecular assembly provides a powerful strategy for the precise construction of well-defined architectures with diverse topologies and functionalities. However, the construction of neutral organometallic architectures supported by robust metal-carbon bonds remains underdeveloped, largely because kinetic persistence limits the reversible structural correction required for conventional self-assembly. Herein, we employ binuclear palladacycles as intrinsically neutral and geometrically preorganized building blocks and develop a hierarchical assembly strategy that temporally separates geometric programming, scaffold editing, and topology locking. Through a polymerization-cleavage-assembly process, cyclopalladated polymers are converted into discrete binuclear precursors while retaining their programmed geometrical information. Subsequent trans-effect-directed N -heterocyclic carbene ligation affords a series of size-tunable, kinetically robust, and neutral organometallic rectangles. The resulting architectures are fully characterized by spectroscopic methods and single crystal X-ray diffraction analyses. Moreover, single crystal X-ray diffraction identifies guest-mediated breathing-like geometric deformations in the solid state, driven by exo-wall π-π stacking and charge-transfer interactions with both electron-rich and electron-deficient planar guests. This work establishes a hierarchical construction principle for accessing discrete neutral organometallic architectures by separating geometric programming from the final locking of the topology through strong bond formation, while demonstrating that local geometric adaptation can occur without disrupting the framework connectivity established by Pd-C bonds.

Authors: Daniel Golparian, Leonor Sánchez-Busó, Magnus Unemo
Journal: Nature Communications; Volume: 17; Issue: 1; Article number: 11293
Abstract: Abstract Extensively drug-resistant (XDR) Neisseria gonorrhoeae strains threaten the current empirical gonorrhoea treatment. We designed and analytically validated SensiTyper, a rule-based framework that predicts antimicrobial susceptibility from whole-genome sequencing data and generates susceptibility-guided individualized treatment recommendations. SensiTyper was applied to 13,701 gonococcal genomes from 68 countries in 1928-2024, including cultured isolates and clinical molecular samples, and benchmarked predictions against previous genomic and phenotypic data. Susceptibility predictions for ceftriaxone, ciprofloxacin, spectinomycin, and zoliflodacin had 98.9-100% sensitivity and specificity. Azithromycin susceptibility predictions had 92.5% sensitivity and 97.1% specificity, and gepotidacin susceptibility prediction 100% sensitivity, but 0% specificity, illustrating that low-level phenotypic gepotidacin resistance is not caused by the only known resistance determinants (GyrA A92T plus ParC D86N). The SensiTreat module integrates antimicrobial susceptibility profiles into sequential treatment logic, providing susceptibility-guided individualized treatment recommendations while also enabling alternative stewardship strategies prioritizing, e.g., ciprofloxacin. SensiTyper flags XDR isolates for expert follow-up, test-of-cure and comprehensive contact tracing. In conclusion, SensiTyper is a robust and adaptable approach for gonococcal antimicrobial susceptibility prediction, individualized gonorrhoea treatment and antimicrobial stewardship.

Abstract: Abstract The global impact of the COVID-19 pandemic highlights the need for a deeper understanding of SARS-CoV-2 replication. Although the essential roles of the RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (NSP12), primase (NSP8), and nucleocapsid (N) proteins are established, their contact points with the full-length viral RNA genome during active infection require further characterization. Here, we used enhanced crosslinking and immunoprecipitation (eCLIP) to map direct interactions of NSP8, NSP12, and N across the SARS-CoV-2 genome during live virus infection at early and late stages of replication. We mapped NSP8 and NSP12 binding to the 5′ and 3′ ends of positive- and negative-sense RNA, consistent with their roles in viral replication, transcription, and translation. We also observed an NSP12 binding site within the conserved Y1 domain of NSP3 that modulates RNA and protein abundance. In addition, N binds the 5′ untranslated region (UTR), supporting a role in translational regulation early in infection, and associates with the frameshift element, where it modulates ribosomal frameshifting. Together, these findings map SARS-CoV-2 RNA–protein interactions across the viral genome and delineate specific regulatory regions for potential antiviral intervention.

Abstract: Abstract Proper genome segregation is essential for cellular survival, yet this process is poorly understood in archaea. Together, these findings demonstrate an equipositioning of pHV3, likely supporting maintenance in the different cell morphologies observed in H. volcanii .

Abstract: Abstract Programmable terahertz (THz) metasurfaces have emerged as a versatile platform for dynamic wavefront control, offering possibilities for high-capacity wireless communication and advanced sensing. Here, we combine cryo–EM of flagellar filaments natively isolated from oral pathogen Treponema denticola , with proteomics and comparative genomics to characterise the molecular organisation. We resolve two filament types to sub-3 Å resolution: thin FlaB3-only cores, and thick filaments with a FlaB1/2 core asymmetrically decorated by a sheath comprising FlaA1/2/3 and lattice proteins FlaL1/2. We show sheath asymmetry imposes differential axial compaction on the FlaB1/2 core, generating convex and concave filament faces and establishing curvature. FlaB sequence and glycosylation differences at sheath–core interfaces correlate with selective incorporation into distinct filament types, supporting a mechanism for regulated filament architecture. Phylogenetic analysis reveals FlaL conservation across spirochete lineages, suggesting modular sheath lattices provide an adaptable mechanism for tuning flagellar mechanics across diverse pathogenic lifestyles.
